passage: On Monday Ujjwal, two, held a banana to his ear and said, "Hello, Mama!" Parveen laughed and took the "call." On Wednesday she told him, "Hop like a bunny!" and he hopped, delighted. On Saturday a neighbour said, "It's raining cats and dogs." Ujjwal ran to the window, looked at the sky, and asked, "Cat? Dog?" Parveen said, "It's raining a lot." He looked unconvinced.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal use as a telephone on Monday?
qa.a: He used a banana.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's question at the window suggest he felt, and what other reading is there?
qa.a: He was probably curious and a little puzzled, since he took the idiom literally, looked at the sky and still looked unconvinced. He might also just have been playing along.

qa.q: What could Parveen do with a toddler when using sayings?
qa.a: She can say what she means in plain words and enjoy pretend games together.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see what happened?
qa.a: The neighbour probably meant nothing but the weather and may find it funny that a small child took her words at face value.

grounding: A toddler understands words literally and uses a banana as a phone, enjoys hopping like a bunny, but takes an idiom at face value.

passage: "Hold your horses, Hemant," said Raghav, as the boy tugged at his shirt at the flat door. Hemant, two, looked around the hall. "Horse?" he asked. "No horse, I mean wait." "Horse gone." Later he picked up the TV remote, put it to his ear and said, "Hello, Papa?" Raghav answered the call. Then Raghav said, "Hop like a frog," and Hemant hopped in circles, giggling.

qa.q: What did Hemant use as a phone?
qa.a: He used the TV remote.

qa.q: What does Hemant's search for the horse suggest he felt, and what might be another reading?
qa.a: He was probably puzzled, since he took the saying literally and looked around the hall for a real horse. He might also have been copying the word without much understanding.

qa.q: What could Raghav do to help Hemant?
qa.a: Raghav can say plainly what he means and keep the pretend games, which Hemant enjoys.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Raghav's answering the remote call?
qa.a: He probably feels understood and enjoys sharing the pretend with Raghav. 😊

grounding: A toddler understands words literally and pretends an object is a phone, enjoys hopping like an animal, but idioms mean nothing yet.

passage:
Joseph picked up a banana and held it to his ear. "Hello? Hello?"
"Who's calling?" asked his uncle Sumit.
"Nani!" Joseph handed him the banana.
"Hello, Nani!" Sumit said into it. Joseph laughed.
Rain hammered the window. "It's raining cats and dogs," said Sumit.
Joseph ran to the window and pressed his nose to it, looking hard. "Cat?" he asked, puzzled.

qa.q: What did Joseph use as a phone?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: Why did Joseph look for cats at the window?
qa.a: He took Sumit's words literally and was curious, then puzzled, when he couldn't find any cats.

qa.q: What could Sumit say to help Joseph?
qa.a: Something simple like, "No cats, just lots of rain," since Joseph can't understand sayings yet.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel watching Joseph search?
qa.a: He probably finds it funny and sweet, and realises Joseph took him literally.

grounding: A toddler enjoys pretend play with a banana phone but takes an idiom literally.

passage: Playgroup note, Friday. Imran loved our animal song. When I said "hop like a bunny," he hopped all round the rug, laughing. When I said "slither like a snake," he lay on his tummy and wriggled. But at tidy-up, when I said, "Hold your horses, Imran," he stopped and looked around the room, frowning. There were no horses. I said, "I mean wait a moment," and he nodded. Dhruv, playgroup teacher

qa.q: What did Imran do when asked to slither like a snake?
qa.a: He lay on his tummy and wriggled.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he looked around the room frowning?
qa.a: He was puzzled, looking for horses, because he took the words literally.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped Imran?
qa.a: Dhruv explained the saying in plain words, "I mean wait a moment".

qa.q: How might Imran's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would probably find it funny and enjoy seeing how literally he takes words.

grounding: A teacher notes a toddler enjoys animal pretend but takes an idiom literally, then explains it plainly.

passage:
Pallavi sat by the village water pump, stirring leaves in a tin with a stick. "Cook," she told her doll, and held a leaf to its mouth.
Her brother Abhinav came in from the field. "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse!"
Pallavi stopped stirring. She looked at him, then at the buffalo in the yard, eyes wide and worried.
"Just a saying," Abhinav laughed. "I'll eat your leaf curry."

qa.q: What was Pallavi cooking in the tin?
qa.a: Leaves, stirred with a stick.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi look worried at the buffalo?
qa.a: She took Abhinav's words literally and was worried he really meant to eat an animal.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that helped?
qa.a: He laughed kindly, explained it was just a saying and joined her pretend play.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel seeing her worried look?
qa.a: He likely finds it funny and sweet, and feels fond of her.

grounding: A toddler plays at cooking but takes her brother's saying literally, and he explains and joins her pretend.

passage:
In the Johannesburg flat, Zanele held a banana to her ear. “Hello! Hello, Gogo!”
Marek, her father, laughed. “Tell Gogo I said hi.”
Then he put on music. “Hop like a bunny!” Zanele hopped, giggling, hands up like ears.
Rain started hammering the window. “Wow, it's raining cats and dogs,” said Marek.
Zanele ran to the window and pressed her nose to the glass, searching. “Where doggy?”
Marek crouched beside her. “No doggies. Just lots of rain."

qa.q: What did Zanele hold to her ear as a phone?
qa.a: She held a banana to her ear.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when she ran to the window looking for the dogs?
qa.a: She was excited and curious, taking the words literally and expecting to see real dogs, which shows the saying meant nothing to her yet.

qa.q: How did Marek respond well when Zanele took the idiom literally?
qa.a: He crouched beside her and explained simply, "No doggies. Just lots of rain," without laughing at her.

qa.q: How might Marek feel watching Zanele search the window?
qa.a: He would likely feel amused and tender, realising she heard his words exactly as spoken.

grounding: It shows a toddler treating a banana as a phone and enjoying hop like a bunny, while taking an idiom literally.
